Attaboy's consistently been one of the best cocktail bars in the world since it opened, so it needs no introduction. What you might not know is that they just started hosting cocktail classes, which is what this review is all about!

I spent my 20s and 30s with Milk & Honey and Attaboy as my neighborhood bars. Needless to say, that experience shaped my taste in cocktails. Now that I live in the suburbs, my access to Sam Ross cocktails largely consists of Tip Top cans from Total Wine. And while my local bar makes Paper Planes, it's absolutely not the same. Given that, I figured it's as good of a time as any to start learning how to make great cocktails myself.

And honestly, who better to teach me than the pioneering bartenders at Attaboy? Sam Ross, who invented Penicillin and Paper Plane, taught the very first class himself, which was a two-hour deep dive on Negronis. Matty Clark, who started at Little Branch in 2009 (!) also taught a class and is leading future sessions. There's something special about learning from bartenders who trained under Sasha Petraske and shaped the speakeasy renaissance worldwide. Best of all, Sam was incredibly friendly, generous with his advice, and completely unpretentious. I left both nostalgic for my youth and with actual skills to bring home.

A special shoutout to Nevada Caldwell, who leads events, developed the curriculum, and writes very persuasive personal emails - the kind that convinced me to sign up in the first place!

If I still lived around the corner, you can bet I'd be a regular. If you're local, I hope you consider checking out their new cocktail classes or doing a corporate team-building event there. What a dream!
I really enjoyed my visit, dark speak easy style atmosphere with really cool light bulbs over the bar. Great music, good vibes, and The Penicillin is a must try!

Attaboy is hands down the BEST speakeasy I’ve been to—not just in NYC, but in the entire US! If you love cocktails, do NOT miss this place.

There’s no traditional menu here. Tell the bartender what flavors and spirits you’re in the mood for, and let them work their magic. I gravitated toward whisky-based, chocolate, and fruit-forward cocktails, and every single one was phenomenal. My husband stuck to Old Fashioned- and Manhattan-style drinks, and those delivered too. The bartender absolutely nailed our preferences, crafting delicious cocktails tailored to our individual tastes.

Getting in is part of the experience: knock on the door, and they’ll let you know if there’s a spot available or add you to the waitlist. We visited on a weeknight around 8:30 PM and waited barely five minutes.

I’ll be coming back every single time I’m in NYC. Exceptional bartending, personalized cocktails, and an experience that genuinely lives up to the hype. Do not miss Attaboy!

During this trip, we visited California (including Westminster's Little Saigon), Las Vegas, Seattle, and New York. Along the way, we tried several Vietnamese restaurants in each city. Unfortunately, most of them were disappointing, and after a while, we decided to stop looking for Vietnamese food altogether. Instead, we chose Thai, Japanese, Italian, and Korean restaurants for the rest of our travels.
When we came across this restaurant, we decided to give Vietnamese food in US one last chance, and we are so glad we did. The food was outstanding and tasted authentically Vietnamese.
I ordered the broken rice with grilled pork, and the flavour was absolutely spot on. The pork was perfectly seasoned and cooked just right. My family ordered the spicy beef noodle soup, pho, BBQ pork vermicelli and they were equally impressed. Every dish was delicious and reflected the traditional flavours we had been hoping to find.
We also had the pleasure of meeting the owner, Long. He shared the story of how he started the restaurant and explained the care and dedication that went into developing the menu. He talked about testing recipes, selecting the right spices and ingredients, and refining each dish to ensure it stayed as close as possible to traditional Vietnamese cuisine before adding it to the menu. His passion and commitment were truly inspiring.
Without a doubt, this was the best Vietnamese restaurant we visited in the United States. It became our family's favourite Vietnamese dining experience of the entire trip, and we would highly recommend it to anyone looking for authentic Vietnamese food.

I learned before my visit that kaiseki is all about culinary art. The whole meal unfolds step by step, focusing on ingredient quality, plating and dining atmosphere.
At Rei in SOHO, you can tell the chef puts a lot of thought into every dish. The plating and presentation are thoughtful, and every course is visually pleasing.

Kaiseki is inherently a refined dining style with smaller portions, meant to be savored slowly.
One small regret: my English isn’t fluent enough to have an in-depth chat with the chef about ingredient selection and the ideas behind each dish.

Great for anyone who enjoys slow dining and appreciates culinary aesthetics. If you’re looking for a filling meal or great value for money, you may want to adjust your expectations.

*Rei might be the best restaurant in Manhattan.*

Every single item on the menu feels like the definitive version of that dish. Everything is deeply flavorful, beautifully balanced, and gorgeously plated. Nothing feels like filler, nothing feels like an afterthought, and every new plate becomes your new favorite.

Ive been here a few times, and will be back as often as I can. Cannot recommend enough.

The staff’s tablet was positioned low on their workstation, while we were seated next to them so whenever they bent over to use it, we happened to have a pretty direct view of their backside. 😅 It was just an awkward seating arrangement, so I’d probably recommend the counter seating instead if you have the option.

The pacing was also on the slower side, with quite a bit of time between each course. Our reservation was at 7:30 PM and we didn’t leave until 10 PM, so definitely plan to spend a good amount of time here if you’re doing the kaiseki menu.

One other thing to note is that I had selected a kaiseki set when booking through OpenTable, but when we arrived, we were told the menu had changed a bit, including the pricing. I completely understand that menus and prices can change with seasonal ingredients and other factors, but I would have appreciated seeing the updated information on OpenTable beforehand.

The staff were very friendly and the chefs work hard. The food itself was delicious and authentically Japanese. I enjoyed the flavor combinations and how thoughtfully everything came together. For me, this is more of an occasional luxury than somewhere I’d visit regularly. Two kaiseki sets, two drinks, and an additional à la carte dish came to over $400.

I probably won’t be returning anytime soon, mainly because of the price and the amount of time involved, but I would still recommend it if you’re looking for a special Japanese dining experience and don’t mind the price or leisurely pace.

I used to frequent The Delancey years ago and always had a great experience. Unfortunately, after attending an event here a few months ago, it's clear that management has taken this place in a very different direction, and not for the better.

There are prominent signs stating that a 20% gratuity is automatically included and non-negotiable. I have a real problem with this policy. Gratuity should reflect the quality of service and be left to the customer's discretion, not dictated by management or ownership.

I opted to pay cash, as I've done in NYC bars for decades, expecting a straightforward transaction where I could tip the bartender myself based on the service. Instead, management insisted on adding both sales tax and a mandatory 20% gratuity, even on cash payments. The poor bartender then had to count out exact change, right down to nickels and dimes, while trying to serve an already busy bar. It's an absurdly inefficient system that inconveniences customers and employees alike, all because of a policy imposed by ownership.

To be absolutely clear, this is not a criticism of the bartender. They were excellent, apologetic, and seemed just as frustrated with the policy as we were. This is entirely a management and ownership decision, and they're the ones who should be held accountable.

The irony is that we ended up spending considerably less than we otherwise would have and eventually left for another, more customer-friendly bar. At that establishment, I happily tipped well over 20% because the service warranted it.

I'm not opposed to tipping generously. Quite the opposite. I'm opposed to businesses removing the customer's discretion and forcing their own employees to enforce policies that create unnecessary friction with customers.

Mandatory gratuities should not become the accepted norm in NYC nightlife. Customers have a choice about where to spend their money, and establishments need to understand that policies like this drive business away.

It's disappointing to see a place I once enjoyed lose some of what made it a great NYC bar in the first place. Management should seriously reconsider this approach.

Casino is a beautifully sexy and elegant restaurant, perfectly situated in a pocket of the Lower East Side where time feels delightfully suspended. It sits in one of the few corners of Manhattan that hasn't been homogenized by rapid gentrification. Here, the true spirit of New York's melting pot remains entirely intact. Looking out, you witness a vibrant crossroads of cultures--a rich diversity that is beautifully mirrored in both the neighborhood's people and the exceptional variety of its culinary landscape.

This was my second visit to Casino, and I was eager to return after being blown away by the food, service, and decor the first time. On this second visit, it felt like walking into an entirely different world--in the best way possible. The dining room transported us straight into a 1940s movie, offering a smoky, sexy, and elegant ambiance (minus the actual smoke). My husband and I were celebrating our wedding anniversary, and the team perfectly set the mood by accommodating our request for a red banquette. Our waitress was incredibly warm, friendly, and offered excellent recommendations. When I asked for wine pairings, she seamlessly transitioned us to Daniel, the sommelier. His recommendations were absolutely beautiful, pairing flawlessly with both my appetizer and entree. My only slight disappointment was that he sent our waitress over to pour and sample the wine rather than presenting it himself.  He did drop by at the end of our meal but it was bittersweet.

My husband and I had a mixed culinary experience here, marked by some disappointing appetizers but truly exceptional pasta dishes.

The Grilled Prawns with Calabrian Chili: We were both pretty underwhelmed by this dish. It lacked the vibrant punch we were expecting.  The Funghi Fritti (Tempura Battered Mushrooms): Honestly, these were awful. They were literally rock-hard, and no amount of lemon aioli or Calabrian chili sauce was going to rehydrate them. The Main Courses: Bucatini with Clams: My husband opted for this and thought it was delicious. The sauce was absolutely gorgeous; his only minor critique was that he wished there had been a bit more of it.  I ordered the Tagliatelle Bolognese: This was the absolute star of the night. It was, without a doubt, the best Bolognese I have ever had in my life.

We highly recommend this hidden gem!

P.S. The hostess checked on every table except ours.

Second, is where it gets scammy:
The sign in front says happy hour tacos $5.

We got others expecting to pay the prices listed next to each item. When we got the check nothing matched prices listed for items. In fine print at the bottom of the happy hour menu outdoor prices are actually $2 more PER ITEM. That means 3 gubenador tacos ordered on happy hour is $33 but just $30 on regular menu. When I spoke to the front desk, I was told my room wasn’t ready because the previous guest had a late check-out, and that my personal request for robes and slippers—which I had submitted three weeks in advance—was causing an additional delay.

When I asked for an ETA, I was simply told to come back in 20 minutes. I returned around 3:30pm and spoke with another staff member who gave a vague answer. Given the inconvenient delay that nearly made me late for an uptown reservation at 5pm, I asked if a late check-out could be accommodated for my departure day. I was told they couldn't approve it at the desk and I’d have to call down later. No gesture or accommodation was offered to alleviate the inconvenience, making for a poor first impression.

To top it off, when I finally got to the room, the robes and slippers I requested three weeks prior were missing. When I asked about them later that evening, I was told they were completely out of slippers, though we did eventually receive the robes.

On a positive note, the room itself was clean. However, noise traveled easily through the door and you could hear people talking in the hall, making it less than peaceful.

Ultimately, I’ve had much better service and hospitality at other New York City hotels, and unfortunately, I will not be returning.

I attended an event here tonight and was accused of stealing FREE merchandise.
When I walked in, a friendly staff member at the name tag table encouraged me and other attendees to check out the stickers at the table perpendicular to hers. I watched several people ahead of me take merchandise from that table, and when it was my turn, I did the same. I want to emphasize this was FREE merchandise — just like the food and matcha drinks being handed out elsewhere at the event, which nobody else was questioned about.
As I zipped up my bag, a staff member approached me and said, "I was not allowed to put that in my bag." I was confused and asked, "You mean the FREE gear we were just told we could take?" He replied, "I have to go check in to see if YOU can have that."
I was understandably offended. I had just watched other people take the same items, and I'd been explicitly told it was for everyone. I waited while he went to "verify" something that had already been made clear. He came back and confirmed, with total confidence, what I already knew.
What made it worse: I recognized this same staff member from earlier, stationed by the door. When another guest in line asked him why there were two lines, he said he didn't know and pointed down the block to someone else as the "point person."
Being singled out and accused like this put a real damper on an event I'd been looking forward to. I'm not writing this review because I was mistaken for a moment — I'm writing it because instead of a simple apology, he doubled down and made me feel like I was in the wrong. In hindsight, I should've escalated it on the spot, but the staff already looked overwhelmed managing the line, and I didn't want to make a scene over stickers.
I enjoyed the rest of the event and didn't let his weaponized incompetence ruin my night. But I won't be back ,  my loss, I guess.

I have always judged falafel against my great-aunt Victoria’s version. I first tasted hers as a preteen, when she stayed with us for several days. She spoke only Arabic and understood a little Spanish, thanks in part to the telenovelas she loved watching. Somehow, we managed to communicate just fine. She cooked up a storm of Lebanese food that week. It was heaven. But she also ruined falafel for me for more than three decades. Try as I might, I could never find a comparable version. They all fell short. By a mile. Until one crisp, picture-perfect autumn day in New York’s NoHo neighborhood. I was shopping in the nearby East Village when I asked the store clerk for lunch recommendations. She rattled off a couple of options, but I stopped listening after she mentioned a place serving Arabic food. A few decades on, I was still on the quest for the falafel against which all others were measured. Naturally, it was on the menu. A steal at $13. It’s street food, cheap to make and never something you should pay a fortune for. I am eternally hopeful, but when it comes to falafel, my optimism doesn’t exactly spring eternal. The cashier was friendly. I would later learn he was the owner’s nephew. In the kitchen stood a man and a woman, both short in stature and of undetermined origin. I remember little else, because the moment I took my first bite, I heard the angel chorus. While no two dishes can ever be exactly alike, nothing has come closer to Victoria’s falafel than the one at Shifka. Trust me, I’ve left quite the wake of half-eaten falafel in my life. I told everyone in the shop as much that day and nearly leapt over the counter to kiss the cooks. I will never not visit now whenever I’m in New York. Heck, I may start staying in the neighborhood for easier access. 10/10! Two thumbs up! Five stars! Shifka has restored my faith in falafel. Victoria would be proud, and undoubtedly approve. Alas, my quest has ended!

Not only the best Smash Burgers in NYC, but the best I’ve had in all 40 States I’ve visited thus far. Incredible Milkshakes as well! Run, don’t walk, to Stash Burger!
Beautiful food workers and good in every way

Stash Burger is seriously worth checking out if you’re in the west village and soho area. I had the Vault Burger and it was incredible — easily one of the better burgers I’ve had in NYC. The burger itself was juicy, flavorful, and the whole combination of the bacon jam and fried onions just worked.

What made the experience even better was getting to speak with the owner. He was genuinely one of the nicest and most down-to-earth people I’ve met at a restaurant. You can tell there’s a lot of passion behind what they’re doing, and that made me want to support the place even more.

If you’re around west village and soho keep Stash Burger in mind. It’s the kind of spot that’s easy to overlook if you don’t know it’s there, but absolutely worth making a stop for. Get the Vault Burger — you won’t regret it. 🍔🔥
The guy behind the counter was super friendly. Turnaround was quick and the Vault Burger was special as in unique and really tasty. I'll be back!

This used to be one of my favorites spots that I recommended to many people but no more… the price of omakase went up significantly and with no real justification. Rice is completely bland and once I mentioned this to chef, instead of expressing some sort of disappointment or concern about what I pointed out , she went on to teach me how it’s more important to focus on fish than rice. Everybody knows that’s not true as the true secret to great sushi is rice. It was rude, I cut the losses after 3 courses and went to another place for dinner with my friend. Very disappointing but there is plenty of places to go in this great city.

Definitely the most recent posts have a point; rice is bland, fish is pre-cut, there was a tomato topping that made it feel cheap. Bring Your Own Sake is a plus and the chef was real nice (even though she was by herself)

Very mediocre pieces and experience for the price. Sushi pieces were plain or had cheap garnishes like tomato or kiwi - no uni or caviar garnishes. For $98 pp it’s not worth the price - you can find better omakase priced at $55-69 in the area
Staff were lovely but sushi was really disappointing, recent reviews say they have recently changed management which may be true. Rice tasted weird and portions are tiny even for omakase
Un’esperienza fantastica, il locale è piccolo ma accogliente e il pesce è veramente di primissima qualità. Personale gentile, prezzi perfetti per la zona in cui si trova. Una meravigliosa scoperta!!
Cozy, great food, reasonable prices.
I really love this little spot.  It’s the perfect hole in the wall.  The food is delicious and the whole experience is lovely.  It is not over done.  I love it.

Such an awesome speak easy in LES / Chinatown. Love the Japanese inspired cocktails and the vinyl music. Difficult to get in on a weekend but regular weeknights were easy to get a drink and chat comfortably.

Nate is an absolutely exceptional bartender. I and my (now) wife went on our first date here and he has been serving us ever since. I would recommend the bottle of Miyo sake, but the Peach Oolong Punch or the cocktail that has oat milk are just so good too. 10/10 cocktails, 10/10 service, 10/10 experience. cannot recommend more.
Favorite bar in NYC
The best!!! Zach is the best!!! Amazing drinks and great atmosphere!!!

This is one of the coolest places in New York City. The drinks are great, and a soft Japanese jazz track plays in the background. You may have to wait a bit to get a seat but both times I’ve been here, two seats opened up within 30 minutes. Fabulous
really lovely, quintessentially new york feel and probably the best fries and fried artichokes I've ever had.

Please get the Cyan-Toni

A cozy witchy apartment with some fun drinks!

PappaRich is a Malaysian restaurant in LES, focused on bringing authentic Malaysian dishes to the NYC area.

We tried a few of the dishes, all of which had a nice strong flavor. Our favorite was the roti, which wasn't dry and paired well with most of the sides that accompanied it. All of the other dishes were pretty standard and reminded us of other Malaysian places we've tried.

Popped in on a chilly day and we were greeted warmly with the smell of delicious food and kind service. The woman who took our order was a delight and very helpful! The white hot coffee and curry was perfect for a wintery day. Would definitely recommend if you are in the area!
Samiha is the best hostess. So kind so sweet

I went for a late night meal after a concert. Wow the hospitality and vibe was unwatched. Samiha was exceptional at accommodating our large order. She was absolutely the best and we had such a great time. I would recommend this to anyone looking for a nice lunch or a late night bite absolutely the best place ever.

3/10 > A spacious café with a simple interior, great for catching up with friends or getting some work done. Unfortunately, the food was a major disappointment.

I came specifically for their sushi tacos and signature crème brûlée sando, only to find the latter sold out. The cream sando was underwhelming—the cream tasted flat and lacking the richness and silky texture you’d expect. The shrimp tempura sushi taco was awkwardly oversized and difficult to eat, with far too many vegetables and barely any rice.

At around $10 per item, the quality simply doesn’t justify the price. Great concepts and presentation, but disappointing execution. Until the food improves, I wouldn’t recommend making a trip here.

The individual behind the bar had no knowledge of the whiskey he served and couldn’t answer a single question our party asked him. We asked him 6 questions about whiskey ranging from what is your favorite US whiskey? What is your favorite scotch? What is your favorite brandy? What is your favorite bourbon. How about cognac? Irish whiskey? His response was “I don’t know” and he couldn’t elaborate any further nor did he care to. We spent over $300 for a couple of 1 oz pours. If you don’t know just pretend you do. We all know this whiskey is marked up to absolute ridiculous secondary prices and you are taking advantage of that. At least have some passion and knowledge of your business. Whiskey was great but the bartender could have been a lot better.

Copper & Oak is an absolute sanctuary for whiskey lovers right in the heart of the Lower East Side. If you appreciate a good pour, this place is a must-visit. The vibe is perfectly rustic and cozy dim lighting, exposed brick walls, and the rich, oaky scent of aged spirits hit you the moment you walk in. It feels like a hidden speakeasy dedicated entirely to the art of whiskey.

The whiskey selection is impressive, but the experience was disappointing. Our group of four was turned away because they don’t accommodate groups. We split into pairs and still waited over an hour for seats. By the time we got in, the mood was ruined. If you only accommodate 10 people, you should take reservations. It felt exclusive in a frustrating way.

Best whisky bar I've experienced in the US. I'm a Scotch collector, I wasn't surprised to find all kind of allocated bourbons and ryes (Pappies, Russel's 13, Michter's 10, 20 and what not), but the real gems for me were the superb Scottish independent bottlings and the incredible knowledge of the very gracious bar keeper. Had a wonderful time.

Food was good but pricy. Service very good. Atmosphere very nice. You can have a conversation and hear each other  chicken par is huge so we shared that and a pasta dish each.
Angela is the most amazing server. We are so happy to with the service and the food.Thank you Angela for making our dirty martinis.. filthy ;) Shes the best!

I loved the food and the service was impeccable!! Honestly, Angela made the entire experience unforgettable. I don’t typically come back to restaurants (NYC has too many I want to try), but just for her I’ll have to. 10/10 experience. Get the chicken parm and chase it down with an espresso martini

Angela was amazing! She was super attentive, friendly, and made sure we had everything we needed throughout our visit. You can tell she genuinely cares about providing great service and making sure her guests have a wonderful experience. Thank you, Angela, for making our visit even better! If you’re looking for a top-tier pizza spot, look no further. We tried a half-and-half custom order: Parma with marinara and prosciutto crisp on one side, and the Shroomtown on the other. Beyond the unforgettable food, the hospitality was phenomenal. Manuel welcomed us with the warmest smile and made delicious cocktails that made our evening extra special. Highly recommended!
Delicious and easy to order, as I wanted a quick dinner to takeout.

((4.5 stars))

stopped by this newish Spunto location a couple of months of go, I think. this location is huge and high-ceiling. this is very much a sit-down restaurant not a pizzeria--having a classic casual interior with a large bar and lots of seating options throughout. the space is very clean and maintained well with a welcoming vibe. had a little time for lunch in the early afternoon and wanted something comforting but also relatively light. pretty familiar with Spunto's style of pizza as they serve this style of pizza at Gruppo, Porto, and Vezzo (other pizza restaurants they own in NYC). while the vibe is classy casual, this place very much feels like a spot for residents and other local workers to enjoy. opted for one of the lunch specials to-go which was  2 plain cheese pizza slices for $5 (not sure if this is a constant special or just for its opening phase). the pizza is consistently good imo as it is extremely thin crust, topped with a flavorful sauce of sweet and salt notes, and topped with super melty mozzarella. beyond the crust being thin, it is somewhat crisp while being light airy. the crust has some flop to it making it easily foldable, the two slices hit the spot as i wanted something somewhat light but also comforting. i’d liken the Spunto’s pizza to a tavern style pizza.  though it is very much a restaurant that mainly serves pizza pies and beyond like pasta options and salads—despite being able to buy slices via a special at lunch. the service was smooth and friendly. my order was boxed up nicely. definitely would stop here again and actually sit down for a meal as this place seems like a good place for group outings.

I must say that the experience I had at Flowing Space Tea house was quite the experience! Ava was so kind and knowledgeable about the teas and gave exceptional service!! She made my experience here worth it, to the point that I plan to come back!!  This is such a cute gem, I recommend everyone to go and experience the ambiance ✨✨

We had an amazing experience here doing the team omakase, the attention to detail was incredible at every step. They led us through each tea, when they would be best consumed, and the key notes that each one contains.The pairings of snacks and some small food items were great and well timed throughout the process, and the "main tea" that was refilled consistently alongside each of the other teas was delightful as well.

The aspect that I appreciated most was all of the incredible glassware and ceramics that not only we used to consume each item, but also the presenters used as they prepared each tea. Each tea was presented with a different tea set, and there was even a beautiful glass apple used to keep the lids of the tea pots off the table.

I would highly recommend trying the tea omakase experience, but you should also check out just the ceramics and sets they offer in-store. The downstairs has a less involved, but still very relaxing, tea shop is something that I definitely plan to return to.

My partner and I went on a 14 course tea omakase journey and it was filled with unique teas and a wonderful conversation with the owner! She really welcomed us in with open arms and was able to give a breakdown of how all the tea leaves are picked and processed.  You learn so much throughout each sip, bite, and there’s even a little whiskey involved too.

The food to pair was delicious and a perfect balance to the different teas.  You get to try white, black, yellow, and green teas prepared both in a cold and hot brew.  A little something for everyone and if you’re a tea lover or just dipping your toes in a must try experience as I’m sure you will get to try something you may have not had before!
Such a unique and relaxing tea experience! The tea and food were delicious, and the staff were very friendly. Highly recommend

Dim sum was very good.

Siu mai - very bouncy meat, mushrooms were fresh. Loved that the skin was moist and not too thick.

Har gow - wrapper is quite thick, but shrimp was fresh and good.

Steamed pork ribs - very good, tender. Not too porky. Liked the pumpkin accompaniment too.

Turnip cake - this was freshly steamed. Tasted amazing. Soft on the inside and crispy on the outside.

Chicken feet - the only let down as the one I got was dried out, probably stayed at the top of the baskets for too long.

Sesame ball - decent with lotus paste.

Tofu pudding - this was very good as well. Went down smoothly with the syrup. Does not have a bitter soy taste.

Chrysanthemum tea - has hot chrysanthemum tea which I love.

Super crowded on a weekend morning/afternoon so be prepared to queue unless you arrive after 2pm.

Place is new-ish and very comfortable. Loved the windows and mirrored ceilings.

Price was reasonable.

Service is good and efficient. Loved the host who was organized and accurate in doling out table numbers, which helped enable a fair system compared to the messy check in experience of other dim sum restaurants.

This is my favorite dim sum restaurant in Manhattan Chinatown. The portion sizes for the rice noodle dishes are gigantic! Great value for the money to be honest. Try to arrive by 11:30am if you want a reasonable wait time. The earlier, the better.

The regular dim sum dishes were fine - my only complaint is the beef meatballs and beef rice noodle seems non existent. You kind of need to pounce on the food carts Guangzhou/Hong Kong style if you want specific food cuz they're just gone by the time the cart gets to you.

Ordered: sugar snap peas, tuna tartare, little gem caesar, glass of Corsican white wine, glass of ‘La Robe d’Ange’ chilled red.
I didn’t love the white, which couldn’t really hold up to our food. Would have been better solo sipping. Chilled red was perfectly fine.
Tuna tartare was the standout—tender, sea-salty, spicy—I could have eaten this all evening.
Caesar dressing was delicious, creamy, anchovy-forward.
Sugar snap peas on the plate was mostly a tangle of midi-greens. The few bites with pea, feta, and ramp were wonderful.
Overall some lovely mouthfuls.

The wine list here is excellent but the real star is the food, which is bold and generous and robustly seasoned but still in harmony with the wine, with all sorts of refined, thoughtful touches that take it beyond the usual cliches of wine bar food into far more exciting culinary territory. We had the charred romano beans, the jimmy nardellos, the tuna tartare with crispy rice pearls, the crab bucatini, the chicken with chermoula, the wagyu picanha, and the pork chop, and they were all fantastic. There’s a real authority to the cooking here — it deserves far more recognition than it’s currently getting.

UPDATE July 2026: Came back again last night and the food is even better than it was the first time. The whole fish is insanely good, as are the lamb chops. There’s such generosity, refinement, and flavor in the cooking here, it blows my mind the chef is not getting more recognition. The server said the restaurant will be closing soon, which seems bizarre given how popular the place is and how good the food is. I hope I’m able to eat this chef’s food again soon — they are a genius!
Guys, food is really amazing, but the noise kills it all.. you’re going out from this with a headache. They really really have to fix this!!

This place is  boring ! BORING and stiff and condesending ! We walked in and its a non standing bar. (lots of rules here-if you like to drink high priced wine in a place that tells you all the things they can’t do for you.This is your spot!)  This kind of place makes me miss the wine bars of Paris where people gather around a bar the same size as this place and they sit and or stand and laugh,talk and hang out FUN!!!.I am so sick of these types of precious , boring places that are killing New York bar/restaurant culture .What we got here (3 of us) from the frosty hostess is the bar is sitting only , she then said we could sweeze in to a banquette but we only have 20 minutes. I say this to my beloved city that I have walked and drank and ate and lived since 1980…what happened to the word YES!!!!Please boring places go home ! This place is backed by hedgefund people. They fail(and this place will) and the somm “owner” will open another boring place with someone new who needs a write off.Go to places that want your business!

A small downtown wine bar with quite enjoyable food. The wine list was decent with reasonable price, and the food was delicious, especially their pasta. Crab bucatini with smoked trout roe was really good, roasted garlic rigatoni had a predictable but good flavor with generous use of Parmesan. Gem lettuce Caesar salad was a bit disappointing- nothing wrong but quite average with only a few lettuce leaves. Hamachi crudo with cucumber and yuzu was refreshing and well balanced in acidity, yet the fish could have been a little firmer in texture- felt a bit mush.
Interior decor appears outdated. Wood burl veneer and square mirror wall panels looked tired and didn’t quite deliver neither a sense of classic nor a contemporary. The noise level is problematic. Even understanding it’s a wine bar, it was really loud and people were shouting to converse. Low ceiling and hard surface furniture seemed bouncing the sounds a lot.

Such a special experience! sitting at the bar immediately transported me to Tokyo. Cocktails were refined and thoughtful. Snacks were amazing, especially the elevated, super delicious chicken tender. For $59 this is one of the few New York experiences I’d call a bargain. Amazing price for such a wonderful evening. Thank you, we can’t wait to come back.

I liked the room, which is annoying in retrospect. It was small, a little cramped, and full of the kind of references I grew up around in family restaurants. For a minute it felt quaint, familiar, like somebody’s actual kitchen. The meal did not survive that impression.

We had come for the fusion, that New York meeting of Hispanic and Chinese food, which is hardly a wild idea in this city. You would think someone in the building could talk about it. The waitress could not. Questions got hesitant, flummoxed half-answers, with no opinion and no sense of what was worth ordering. She set the plates down and left. Water was not refilled. A premade iced tea and a straw took about ten minutes. We were in the back booth by the bathroom, along one narrow walkway, so there was nowhere for her to pretend she was not passing us. She did, ten or twelve times, without a word, clearly clocking whether we were done. In a room that small, a stare is not subtle. The attention arrived for the exit and never for the meal. It felt scrutinized, and a little discriminatory.

The portions were generous for the price, and that is the only credit I will give. The food was greasy, overcooked, and mushy, oversalted and still underseasoned, with a gamey edge that belonged to neither tradition. The broccoli beside the sesame chicken was the best thing on the table, which is a miserable thing to have to admit. Everything else tasted like a five-minute search for the dish it was supposed to be. A bastardization. The drinks were the same failure in a glass: too tart and sour, or so sweet the fruit had disappeared.

I can speak for the Chinese side. The people with me can speak for the Hispanic side. None of us took this as gospel, and none of us were impressed. This city already has rooms that love both cuisines, and rooms that fuse them without embarrassing either one. This was the neighborhood worn as a costume. An overrated cash grab, with none of the love and none of the craft. I would not go back.

I’m curious if the next owners of the space will keep the deep red paint. I kind of like it.

Honestly an 11/10 experience on all fronts. The ribeye is hands down the best steak I've ever had. The wedge salad, chicken, burger. The simplicity of the pasta shows culinary depth. Add in great service in a beautiful room. Highly recommend. Very special place

So where do I begin. The classic “we’ll seat you once your full party arrives.” Fair enough. We wait, only to watch another incomplete party get seated ahead of us.

Naturally, we ask why. “Oh, because they said the rest of their party is right around the corner.”

…Which is exactly what we said. But okay, we move on.

We finally sit down and are greeted with the wine and drinks menu. Lovely. Except it takes another 30 minutes for the actual food menu to make an appearance.

When we finally order, we ask our waiter what he’d recommend. His response? “I tend to order steak at a steakhouse…” ...is romy a steakhouse? He then proceeds to tell us that the amount of food we’ve ordered is laughably small. So, against our better judgment, we add a steak.

The food arrives at a glacial pace, and by the time we’re finished, we’re painfully full. Everything is incredibly rich and creamy, and we’re left wondering why we were so persuaded to order more food in the first place.

The restaurant itself is beautiful. I just wish the experience had lived up to the setting.
Amazing service and incredible food!!
Great pizza !

La Pizza Napoli is a hidden gem. Their margarita pizza is amazing. I love their pizza by the slice option, and genuinely affordable prices for being in Manhattan. But the thing that stood out the most to me was how lovely the staff were. They took such excellent care of me, and were genuinely so patient and understanding with all customers. I wish the owner much success, and hope he expands to more locations.

Another hyped restaurant. I was really excited to try this place. My Malawach was burnt and I like well done. It didn't taste homemade. It was flat and dry. Hummus and dips weren't all that good but homemade bread was delicious. The server was on her phone or chatting with other servers.  Had to be flagged down for anything. NO GRADE LETTER ON THE WINDOW!! Definitely missed that or I wouldn't eat there. $200 lunch for 2 without alcohol. I wouldn't mind for delicious food but this wasn't it.
Great place for dinner. The food was amazing and our server Jonathon was very nice and helpful!
